content: Healthcare providers should prioritize not only the needs and values of patients but also those of their families. Core values of primary healthcare (PHC) include equity, social justice, universality, people-centeredness, community protection, participation, scientific soundness, personal responsibility, self-determination, and self-reliance, as outlined by the World Health Organization (WHO). Globally, at least 400 million people lack access to essential health services, largely due to the focus on expensive, disease-specific programs, insufficient resources for PHC (including community-based palliative care), and poor integration between vertical programs and PHC. With aging populations and the increasing burden of chronic illnesses and multimorbidities, fragmented healthcare systems are struggling to meet the growing demand for care. These conditions include cancer, organ failure, HIV/AIDS, and mental health disorders such as depression, dementia, and substance use disorders. Integrated, accessible, and people-centered PHC has been improved in some countries through the integration of social services, such as housing, employment, family welfare, and disability support programs. Addressing social determinants of health and alleviating social suffering through such programs is fundamental to both PHC and palliative care, highlighting their interconnectedness. Evidence shows that most people prefer to spend the final phase of their lives at home. To honor this preference and reduce hospital overcrowding, palliative care must be available in the community and in patients' homes. Pain relief and palliative care programs should be incorporated into existing healthcare systems, ensuring accessibility at home. Primary care clinicians with basic palliative care training, along with simple, safe, effective, and affordable medicines and equipment, can meet the palliative care needs of most patients. However, systems should be in place to allow primary care clinicians to consult with specialists for complex cases and to transfer patients to higher-level institutions when necessary. Integrated palliative care within PHC has been shown to be both high-quality and cost-effective, even in low-income countries. It can reduce healthcare costs by decreasing reliance on hospital services and provide financial risk protection for families. Community health workers (CHWs) and volunteers can play a vital role in palliative home care, fostering social solidarity and cohesion. Specialist palliative care physicians are essential in every country to serve as teachers, advisors, and providers for the most complex cases. However, the majority of palliative care needs can be met by general practitioners, family physicians, or non-physician healthcare workers with basic palliative care training. Task-sharing and task-shifting within PHC have proven to be safe and effective ways to improve access to services, including the management of chronic illnesses, mental health conditions, and pain relief. Universal health coverage (UHC) cannot be achieved without universal access to PHC, which includes community-based palliative care. This care must address pain and symptom control, psychosocial support, and home care for patients with serious or life-threatening illnesses, while also providing financial risk protection for their families. The Essential Package of Palliative Care for PHC, as recommended by WHO, includes safe, effective, and affordable medicines, simple equipment, basic social supports, and trained human resources. This package aims to prevent and relieve suffering of all types—physical, psychological, social, and spiritual. Medicines such as oral and injectable morphine, haloperidol, and fluoxetine are critical for managing pain, nausea, anxiety, and depression. Social supports, including food packages, housing assistance, and transportation vouchers, are necessary to meet the basic needs of patients and their families. Healthcare providers should also address the spiritual needs of patients and families, facilitating access to culturally appropriate spiritual counseling. CHWs can play a crucial role in palliative care by visiting patients at home, providing emotional support, identifying unmet needs, and reporting findings to supervising clinicians. Family caregivers, often women living in poverty, should be trained and supported to provide basic nursing care while their own social needs are assessed and addressed. For patients nearing the end of life, the focus of care should shift to comfort and quality of life. Families should be supported to be present during this time, and spiritual support should be made available as needed. Social supports, including assistance with funeral costs, should be accessible to families living in extreme poverty to alleviate financial and emotional burdens. In summary, integrating palliative care into PHC is essential for improving patient outcomes, reducing healthcare costs, and promoting UHC. This requires a comprehensive approach that includes training healthcare providers, ensuring access to essential medicines and equipment, addressing social determinants of health, and supporting patients and their families in their communities.
